nameStory: The green frog earned its straightforward name from the varying shades of green that typically color its head and often much of its body. While not all individuals are bright green - some lean more bronze or brownish - that distinctive greenish head is the feature that gives this common amphibian its simple, descriptive name.
description: The green frog is a medium-sized amphibian that's one of New England's most commonly encountered frogs. True to its name, it usually sports a green head, though the rest of its body can range from green to bronze to brown. These sturdy frogs are smaller than bullfrogs but larger than many of their pond-dwelling cousins, and they're known for being quite territorial, especially the males who guard their watery domains with impressive dedication.

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Look for that telltale green head that gives this frog its name, though the body can be green, bronze, or brownish - the green coloring on the head is usually the most reliable feature

idTips.label: Call
idTips.description: Males produce a distinctive low-pitched 'gunk' or banjo-like 'twang' that sounds like plucking a loose guitar string - quite different from the deep 'jug-o-rum' of bullfrogs

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Skin feels smooth and moist to the touch, typical of aquatic frogs, with prominent ridges (called dorsolateral folds) running partway down the back from behind the eyes

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent golden or bronze-colored eyes that sit high on the head, allowing them to peek above water while mostly submerged

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found in or very near permanent water - ponds, lake edges, slow streams, or marshes where they can quickly dive for safety

habitat: Green frogs stick close to permanent water sources throughout New England, including pond edges, lake shores, slow-moving streams, and marshes. They prefer spots with plenty of vegetation both in the water and along the banks, which provide cover and hunting grounds for insects. Unlike some frogs that only visit water to breed, green frogs are homebodies that rarely venture far from their aquatic territories.

seasonality.spring: Males begin their territorial calling as waters warm, producing their distinctive banjo-like 'gunk' sounds. This is when you're most likely to hear them before you see them.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season with loud calling, breeding, and the most visible frog activity around water edges. Adults are easiest to spot basking or hunting along shorelines.
seasonality.fall: Activity gradually decreases as temperatures drop, but you can still find them on warm days. They begin moving to deeper water for winter preparation.
seasonality.winter: Green frogs hibernate underwater in the mud at the bottom of ponds and streams, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Male green frogs are such dedicated territory defenders that they'll actually wrestle with intruders, grappling and trying to push rivals out of their claimed patch of pond - imagine tiny sumo wrestlers in the water!
confusionNotes: Green frogs are most often confused with bullfrogs, but remember this simple trick: green frogs have ridges (dorsolateral folds) that run partway down their backs from behind their eyes, while bullfrogs have smooth backs without these ridges. Also, green frogs make a banjo-like 'gunk' while bullfrogs make a deep 'jug-o-rum' call.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'green' frogs, don't expect them all to be bright green - the bronze frog is actually a subspecies of green frog that can be quite brownish, which sometimes confuses beginning frog watchers who expect all green frogs to be obviously green.
compareHints: Among its water frog relatives, green frogs are larger than wood frogs and leopard frogs but smaller than bullfrogs, and they're the only ones that consistently show green coloring on the head. Unlike the spotted leopard frogs or the woodland-dwelling wood frogs, green frogs are committed water-dwellers that rarely stray from pond edges, making them easier to predict where you'll find them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the green frog which has prominent ridges down its back and lives near permanent water, wood frogs are smooth-backed forest dwellers.
Bullfrogs are significantly larger than their closest New England relatives like Green Frogs and Wood Frogs, and completely lack the fold-like ridges that run down the backs of Green Frogs.
Unlike the green frog which has prominent ridges running down its back, the pickerel frog's back is smooth between its square spots.
Unlike green frogs which have prominent ridges running down their backs, northern leopard frogs have smooth backs with only faint ridges.
Unlike green frogs which have distinct ridges running down their backs and venture onto land regularly, mink frogs have smoother backs and stick close to water.
Among its leopard frog relatives, the Atlantic Coast leopard frog is most similar to the Northern leopard frog but has a more restricted coastal range.
